holidays.name: National Fruitcake Day
holidays.description: A day dedicated to the dense, candied-fruit-studded loaf that is the most joked-about dessert of the holiday season. Fans celebrate by actually eating it, while skeptics celebrate by regifting it.
holidays.origin: Fruitcake traces back to ancient Rome, where soldiers carried a portable mix of pomegranate seeds, pine nuts, and raisins bound in barley mash. The modern American observance appeared in the late 20th century as a food-calendar holiday meant to rescue the cake's reputation after the holidays.
holidays.funFact: Fruitcake soaked in alcohol can last for years, and a fruitcake left by explorer Robert Falcon Scott in Antarctica in 1910 was found more than 100 years later in surprisingly edible condition.

holidays.name: Visit the Zoo Day
holidays.description: An unofficial day for escaping holiday leftovers and relatives to go see the animals. It encourages people to spend a post-Christmas day with giraffes, penguins, and other creatures that don't ask about your career plans.
holidays.origin: This is a modern, unofficial observance popularized through novelty holiday calendars. It fits the lull between Christmas and New Year's, when families are off work and school and looking for an outing.
holidays.funFact: Many zoos see strong attendance in the week after Christmas, and some animals, like penguins and polar bears, are happy about the cold weather.

holidays.name: Make Cut-Out Snowflakes Day
holidays.description: A crafty winter celebration where everyone folds paper, snips bits out, and unfolds a one-of-a-kind snowflake. It's a cheap, scissor-based way to turn your windows into a blizzard.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial craft holiday tied to the winter season. Paper snowflakes became popular as a simple winter craft in schools and homes, especially in the 20th century.
holidays.funFact: Real snowflakes have six sides because of how water molecules arrange themselves, but most paper snowflakes are folded in a way that makes eight, so they're technically anatomically incorrect.

holidays.name: Spanish Tapas Day
holidays.description: An unofficial food holiday that raises a toast to small plates and shared bites. Gather friends, order too many little dishes, and call it dinner.
holidays.origin: Tapas come from Spain, and legend says the tradition began with bartenders placing a slice of bread or ham over a drink to keep flies out. The word comes from the Spanish verb tapar, meaning to cover.
holidays.funFact: One popular legend claims King Alfonso X of Castile ordered taverns to serve food with wine, so that drinkers wouldn't get too tipsy.

holidays.name: Fruitcake Toss Alternative: Fruitcake Regifting Reflection Day
holidays.description: A tongue-in-cheek unofficial extension of fruitcake season, where people reflect on the sturdy gifts that have circled the globe unopened. Some participants stage fruitcake tosses, catapult contests, or taste tests.
holidays.origin: Fruitcake tossing events grew from humor around fruitcake's durability, with towns across the U.S. hosting contests, such as the one in Manitou Springs, Colorado, which is held in January.
holidays.funFact: Contestants in fruitcake-launching contests have built trebuchets, air cannons, and slingshots to hurl cakes hundreds of feet.
